entities.name: Antiochus I Theos of Commagene
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Antiochus I Theos Dikaios Epiphanes Philorhomaios Philhellen was the king of the Greco-Iranian kingdom of Commagene, a significant Greco-Roman client state in the eastern Mediterranean. Born into the Seleucid dynasty, he ascended to the throne around 69 BCE and ruled until his death in 37 BCE. During his reign, Antiochus I Theos worked to consolidate his power and protect Commagene's interests, navigating complex diplomatic relationships with neighboring kingdoms and empires.

As a key figure in the Hellenistic world, Antiochus I Theos played a crucial role in maintaining the cultural and religious ties between Greece and Asia Minor. He actively promoted the worship of Zeus, a major deity in Greek mythology, and expanded the Commagene kingdom's borders through military campaigns.

Antiochus I Theos's legacy extends beyond his own reign, as he helped to lay the groundwork for the Roman conquest of Pontus and Cappadocia. His successor, Deiotarus II, would go on to play a significant role in the eventual incorporation of Commagene into the Roman Empire.

The Commagene kingdom's rich cultural heritage, which Antiochus I Theos helped to preserve, includes the famous Commagene tombs, adorned with reliefs depicting the king and his family. These monuments showcase the blending of Greek and Persian architectural styles that characterized the Greco-Iranian kingdoms.

In 17 BCE, the Roman general Crassus invaded Commagene, sparking a devastating war that would ultimately lead to the kingdom's incorporation into the Roman Empire. Antiochus I Theos died in 37 BCE, before this event, and was succeeded by his son Deiotarus II.
